\chapter{The Household}
\label{ch:ta-household}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a child, a son, a daughter and the family in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C43-family and say all four words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuḻandai]{\ta{குழந்தை} (kuḻandai) — child}

\label{lesson:TA-C43-child}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{koṭu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{குழந்தை}}
\textbf{\ta{குழந்தை}} (\emph{kuḻandai}) — \textquotedblleft{}child\textquotedblright{}.

Take it apart and the stem is \emph{kuḻa-}, 'young, tender', closed off into a noun by \emph{-ndai}. The same stem stands behind \emph{kuḻavi}, 'infant'. Nothing in the word says boy or girl: it names the age, not the sex.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of four words for the people in a house. Three follow, and each reuses the ones before.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuḻandai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{koṭu}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{குழந்தை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}child\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[makaṉ]{\ta{மகன்} (makaṉ) — son}

\label{lesson:TA-C43-son}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kuḻandai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மகன்}}
\textbf{\ta{மகன்}} (\emph{makaṉ}) — \textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}.

The stem is \emph{maka-}, an old Dravidian word for offspring, and \emph{-aṉ} is the ending Tamil puts on a male person — the same \emph{-aṉ} already sitting on \emph{naṇbaṉ}, 'friend'. So the word assembles in front of you: offspring, then male.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second word for the house, and an ending you had already met elsewhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{makaṉ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{kuḻandai}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மகன்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[makaḷ]{\ta{மகள்} (makaḷ) — daughter}

\label{lesson:TA-C43-daughter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{makaṉ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மகள்}}
\textbf{\ta{மகள்}} (\emph{makaḷ}) — \textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{}.

The same \emph{maka-} stem as the last lesson, with \emph{-aḷ} where that word had \emph{-aṉ}: one ending marks a woman, the other a man. The sibling words you met earlier needed four separate forms to split brother from sister by age; here a single stem does the work of two. Malayalam's \emph{makan} and \emph{makaḷ} match Tamil almost letter for letter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One stem, two endings, two people. One more word closes the chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{makaḷ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{makaṉ}, and hear only the ending move
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மகள்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuṭumbam]{\ta{குடும்பம்} (kuṭumbam) — family}

\label{lesson:TA-C43-family}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{makaḷ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{குடும்பம்}}
\textbf{\ta{குடும்பம்}} (\emph{kuṭumbam}) — \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{}.

The collective word the family lesson never needed, because \ta{அப்பா}, \ta{அம்மா} and the four sibling words each named one particular person. It comes from Sanskrit \emph{kuṭumba}, 'household' — which Sanskrit itself appears to have taken from a Dravidian source before handing it back — and the \emph{-am} on the end is what Tamil gives such borrowings.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: child, son, daughter, and the word for all of them together.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuṭumbam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{makaḷ}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{குடும்பம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
